chat.runtimeSwitch.carryNative: The whole conversation crosses to {{toRuntime}} as its own history, tool calls and their results included. chat.runtimeSwitch.carryNativeCodex: The whole conversation crosses to {{toRuntime}} as model-visible history, with nothing trimmed — tool calls and their results included. Image attachments cross as file paths rather than as images, so {{toRuntime}} has to open them from disk again. What stays behind: the model's own reasoning from before the switch.
chat.runtimeSwitch.carryText: Only a text summary of the most recent messages crosses. Tool calls and their results do not. The model's own reasoning from before the switch does not cross either.
chat.runtimeSwitch.codexThreadStore: Codex keeps its own list of past conversations, and on this app it stays empty on purpose: each session gets a private Codex home that is deleted when the session ends. Your history is kept by Odysseus itself and is the same on every runtime, so nothing is lost by switching.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costAddedFolderSkills: Skills that live in a folder you added to this session stop being loaded — Claude reaches them through its added directories and Codex through its own extra skill roots, but {{toRuntime}} treats an added folder as a setting that loads no skills.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costAppActions: The model can no longer act on the app itself — sources, plugins, the browser pane and skill files.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costAutoCompaction: Turning auto-compaction off stops having an effect: {{toRuntime}} has no switch for it and still compacts the conversation on its own at about 90% of the window.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costAutoCompactionKno: The operator's auto-compaction window and threshold settings stop having any effect — {{toRuntime}} compacts at its own fraction of the model's context window whatever they are set to. Pi uses the values as written; Claude uses them too, but never narrows its window below 100,000 tokens.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costAutoDenialBreaker: A run of refused actions no longer pulls the session out of Auto mode — on {{toRuntime}} the mode never changes on its own, so it keeps auto-running until you change it yourself.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costAutoMemoryDirecto: The folder you chose for auto memory stops covering everything written here: {{toRuntime}} keeps a second auto memory of its own, in its own place, and this app does not move it. Memories it writes there stay outside the folder you picked, and nothing in this app reads them.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costBackgroundTaskOff: An operator's setting turning background tasks off stops applying — {{toRuntime}} has no switch for it, so shell commands can still be left running in the background there. Its only related setting is how long their output is polled for, not whether they start.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costBashWorkingDir: A `cd` inside a Bash call stops carrying over to the next one — on {{toRuntime}} every command starts in the session's own folder again, so a sequence that changed directory and then ran a relative command will not work as written.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costBridgeTools: Scheduled runs, event watches, goals, messages to other sessions, the session's status and labels, page publishing, board tasks and the Pages tools may be missing: on {{toRuntime}} they need a per-session link that is set up when the session starts and can fail to come up.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costClaudeBuiltinAgen: The two agents Claude ships of its own, Explore and Plan, do not exist on {{toRuntime}} — work you delegated to either runs on this session's ordinary agents instead.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costClaudeProjectComm: Custom commands kept in this project's `.claude/commands/` folder stop working — {{toRuntime}} has no reader for that folder, and this app's own command list never showed them either: it reads `.nessy-agent/commands` and `.agents/commands`. Import them from your Claude setup to keep them on every runtime.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costCodexBuiltinAgent: The two agents Codex ships of its own, explorer and awaiter, do not exist on {{toRuntime}} — work you delegated to either runs on this session's ordinary agents instead.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costCodexDetachedRevi: A code review Codex is running in the background is abandoned. It runs on a review thread that belongs to Codex, carrying this app's own diff and review checklist — but the thread does not exist on {{toRuntime}}, so switching while a review is in flight loses it and its findings never arrive. The conversation itself is kept; start the review again after the switch.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costCodexReviewer: Codex's own approval reviewer stops judging escalated actions — {{toRuntime}} has no counterpart for it, and the reviewer policy you wrote is read by nothing there.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costCredentialShellFl: Credential files stop being blocked by the operating system: on {{toRuntime}} they are hidden from the model's search and file-listing tools, but a shell command that walks a folder above them can still read them.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costForkSubagent: Subagents stop inheriting this conversation and its prompt cache — on {{toRuntime}} each one starts from an empty context and pays for its own, where an interactive Pi session forks them by default.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costGatewayFeatureFla: If the Claude connection you are switching to is a Nessy Gateway one, its runtime is deliberately kept off the vendor's network: auto-updates, release notes, availability checks and feature-flag fetching are all off, and background runs of plugin command sources stop. A Claude subscription connection keeps every one of them.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costGuardian: The Guardian safety judge stops reviewing risky actions — in Allow all, nothing on {{toRuntime}} blocks a destructive command or a secret-exfiltration attempt for you.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costHostMcpRules: Permission rules written about a network host no longer bind {{toRuntime}}'s own commands and file edits — those approvals only ever carry a shell command or a file path — and no tool this app runs for it passes through your rules either. A rule naming one MCP tool, a whole MCP server or a pattern still holds there, except over a source that was still connecting when the session started: a tool it adds that its server marks read-only, {{toRuntime}} runs without asking. The session names both kinds.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costLiveToolInput: Tool calls stop filling in as they are written — on {{toRuntime}} a tool's arguments arrive only once the whole call is complete, so a long edit or command appears all at once instead of building up.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costNestedProtectedPa: A protected folder deeper inside the project stops being confirmed with you — a submodule's `.git`, a vendored checkout's `.claude`. {{toRuntime}} protects those names at the top of each working folder and no further down, so a write below that lands without asking. The ones at the top of the project are still confirmed.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costPathScopedInstruc: Instructions that depend on which file is being touched stop arriving: on {{toRuntime}} a CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory is not fetched when the model works there, and a rule or skill scoped to matching paths never activates.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costPlanApproval: Plan mode has no plan to accept: the model cannot hand you one to approve.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costPolicyKeys: 32 documented Claude Code policy and security switches stop having any effect — {{toRuntime}} reads none of them, and nothing tells you when one you set is being ignored.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costPreToolCheck: Odysseus stops checking each action before it runs — {{toRuntime}} decides on its own what to ask you about.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costPreToolDefer: A hook that pauses an action for later stops pausing it — on {{toRuntime}} a PreToolUse hook answering "defer" cannot hold a call open, so the call proceeds or is refused there and then.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costProjectMcpApprova: Approvals you wrote for a project's own MCP servers stop being read — {{toRuntime}} honours none of the three settings keys that turn them on or off, so those servers are decided by this app's own consent instead.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costProtectedFilesUnp: Writes to your shell startup files and to a project's `bunfig.toml` or `pyrightconfig.json` stop being confirmed with you. Pi and Claude ask before one, whether the model uses a file tool or a shell command; {{toRuntime}} has no "ask" for a file at all, and with the sandbox off it runs an ordinary command without telling this app, so the same write lands with no card.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costReadFence: The setting that keeps file reads inside your working folders stops applying — {{toRuntime}} reads with its own built-in tools, which Odysseus never sees before they run, so nothing on this side can refuse a read outside those folders.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costReasoningCarry: Reasoning stops surviving a handoff on {{toRuntime}} unless the connection speaks the Responses API — one running through the gateway has nowhere to put the model's own thinking, so it is dropped. Reasoning never crosses between runtimes in any case, including on this switch.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costRuleSubjects: Permission rules written against anything but a shell command or a file path stop being consulted — when {{toRuntime}} asks to run a command or change a file it can be judged only by Bash, Write and Edit rules carrying a command or a file path, so a rule naming another tool, another parameter or an agent has nothing to match there. The session says which of your rules those are.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costScheduledRun: The model can no longer send you a desktop notification when a long task finishes.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSecurityPluginEnv: The environment variables that turn the security-guidance plugin's layers off stop reaching it. ENABLE_PATTERN_RULES, ENABLE_STOP_REVIEW, ENABLE_COMMIT_REVIEW, ENABLE_CODE_SECURITY_REVIEW and SECURITY_GUIDANCE_DISABLE govern the plugin on Claude, where its hooks run inside the runtime's own child and inherit your whole environment. On {{toRuntime}} those hooks are run by Odysseus and inherit six variables only — HOME, PATH, SHELL, TMPDIR, TEMP and TMP — so an exported switch does nothing and every layer keeps running. The plugin itself is unaffected; to turn a layer off here, set the variable in that hook's own env block.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSessionAgent: The session stops running as the agent you pinned — on {{toRuntime}} there is no main-thread agent, so its instructions, its tool restriction and its opening prompt no longer shape the conversation.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSubagentAgentIdHe: Gateway requests stop saying which subagent made them. The Claude runtime sends an agent id of its own, which Odysseus renames onto the x-nessy-agent-id header; on {{toRuntime}} nothing produces one, so an operator reading gateway logs sees the session and not the agent inside it. The session id itself is still sent.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSubagentMemory: A subagent's own memory does not come along — an agent that learned something here starts empty on {{toRuntime}}. Claude keeps per-agent memory in the SDK's own folder rather than ours, and Codex has no per-agent memory at all.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSubagentNesting: Subagents can no longer start subagents of their own — on {{toRuntime}} the chain stops one level below this conversation, and fewer of them run at the same time.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSubagentOutputTex: A subagent's own output stops being delivered — on {{toRuntime}} a fan-out reports only that each child is still working and how many tools it has called, so a slow subagent and a stuck one look the same.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSubagentReportSca: A subagent's report reaches this conversation unscanned — on {{toRuntime}} nothing checks what a delegated agent writes back for instruction-shaped text and nothing marks it as untrusted, so text it read in a file or on a page can address the model as if the harness had said it.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costSubagentWorktree: A subagent Odysseus would isolate in its own git worktree may run in this session's folder instead — on {{toRuntime}} its edits land straight in your working copy, beside yours.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costToolMemoryCap: A memory cap an operator set for tool commands stops applying — {{toRuntime}} reads no such setting, so a runaway command is bounded by nothing. Claude honours it on Linux and WSL alone, along with the companion setting that widens the same cap to the other kinds of process it starts.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costToolRestriction: A session-level tool restriction stops narrowing what the model may call — {{toRuntime}} honours only part of it, or none. Claude applies both the allowed list and the disallowed one, but its allowed list narrows only the built-in tools and leaves every MCP tool available; Pi's allowed list is the whole tool set, MCP tools included, and Pi silently ignores the disallowed one; Codex cannot express either, because its own enabled and disabled tool lists cover MCP servers rather than built-in tools.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costToolSupportFallba: A model that refuses to accept tools stops moving your fallback chain forward — Pi switches to the next entry on that refusal and {{toRuntime}} does not, so the turn ends instead of being handed on. Codex switches on overload and server failures alone, and the claude binary does not publish which failures move its own chain.
chat.runtimeSwitch.costWorktree: The model can no longer move the session into a separate git worktree — it works straight in your working folder.
chat.runtimeSwitch.crossRuntimeBody: The conversation on screen is kept in full, but {{fromRuntime}}'s working memory does not come along. The reasoning level is not reset — it is lowered to the highest level {{toRuntime}} offers, and permissions are narrowed the same way. Background tasks started by {{fromRuntime}} are stopped.
chat.runtimeSwitch.crossRuntimeBodyCodex: The conversation on screen is kept in full, but {{fromRuntime}}'s working memory does not come along — {{toRuntime}} receives what was said, not what was done, so have it re-check any file or command you depend on. The reasoning level is not reset — it is lowered to the highest level {{toRuntime}} offers, and permissions are narrowed the same way. Background tasks started by {{fromRuntime}} are stopped.

dialog.bypassPermissions.description: In Bypass permissions mode every action runs without approval prompts — file changes, shell commands, and network access included. Use it only in an environment you fully trust. This choice is remembered on this computer.
dialog.bypassPermissions.recommendation: Prefer Auto unless you specifically need the rest: it runs low-risk actions without prompting and still asks before risky ones.
dialog.bypassPermissions.runtimeNote: It does not mean the same thing on every runtime. On Pi and Claude Code it applies to everything the agent can reach. On Codex it is narrower: Codex's own workspace sandbox stays on even in this mode, because the profile this app writes to keep .git and the other protected folders read-only builds on it, so sandboxed writes outside the workspace, the temp folders and any folder you added are still refused. And with nobody attending the session, skipping the prompt is not the same as granting it — a call no rule covers is refused rather than run, unless an operator sets unattendedApprovalFallback to allow. With Codex auto-review on, Codex's reviewer still answers the actions Codex raises in this mode — as Pi's Guardian, when it is on, still screens risky actions in it.

settings.ai.codexAutoReview.enabledDesc: In Auto, and in Bypass permissions as a safety net, when an action would be escalated for approval Codex asks its own reviewer first instead of interrupting you. In Manual and Accept edits it asks you, and the reviewer is never asked in Plan or Don't ask. If your organisation's Codex policy allows only the reviewer, that policy wins: the reviewer answers in Manual, Accept edits and Don't ask too, Codex refuses Plan turns, and the session says so. Off by default. Turning it off applies from the next message in open Codex sessions; turning it on, and a change to the reviewer policy, applies to Codex sessions started afterwards. A denial can be overruled with /approve, and a run of denials interrupts the turn. While it is on, the reviewer can also approve what this app would otherwise refuse or always put in front of you — this app's safety floors (removing your home or root folder among them), the paths you have denied, and any deny rule Codex cannot enforce itself — because Codex asks its reviewer before it asks this app. In Bypass it still answers what Codex raises — as Pi's Guardian still screens risky actions there — and in Auto a change to what an unattended automation does or when it runs is refused instead of reviewed.

settings.ai.decisions.featureAutomationC: Let automations check a yes/no condition before they run.

An automation can carry a condition written as a question, such as "Is the user reporting a bug?". Before the automation starts a session, Jev/Laya answers it from the event and the session's latest messages, and skips the run when the answer is no. Automations without a condition are unaffected.
settings.ai.decisions.featureDecideToolD: Let the agent classify, route and score items with the decide tool. Applies to new sessions.
settings.ai.decisions.featureDecideToolT: The agent can call the decision model (Jev, or Laya on your machine) to classify, route, score or yes/no-check items, for example sorting 200 emails into folders in one call.
settings.ai.decisions.featureMidTurnMess: Decide whether a message sent while the agent works steers it or waits.

When you send a message while the agent is working, Jev/Laya judges whether it corrects the current task (delivered right away) or is a separate follow-up (queued until the task finishes). Queued messages that belong to the same request are sent together as one turn. Without a clear answer the connection's usual behaviour applies.
settings.ai.decisions.featureRiskBadgesD: Tag permission prompts with what the action does.
settings.ai.decisions.featureRiskBadgesT: Before a permission prompt appears, Jev/Laya tags it with what the action does: deletes data, sends data out, publishes, touches secrets, changes the system, or spends money. Informational only: the prompt, its buttons and your choice are unchanged. The prompt's description and command are sent to the decision model.
settings.ai.decisions.featureSemanticLab: Evaluate yes/no auto-apply rules on labels (for example "Is this about billing?") on every message.
Label rules can be yes/no questions such as "Is this about billing?". Jev/Laya answers them for every message you send, and the label is applied when the answer clears the rule's threshold.
settings.ai.decisions.featureSmartTitles: Skip titling small talk and refresh titles when the topic moves on.

When a session starts with small talk such as "hi", Jev/Laya holds the AI title back until you ask for something. Every few messages it also checks whether an automatic title still describes the conversation and refreshes it if not. Titles you set yourself are never changed.
settings.ai.decisions.featureSuggestions: Point the agent at a skill or source your message plainly needs.

Before a message is handled, Jev/Laya compares it with your skills and with sources that are set up but not active in this session. When one clearly fits, the agent gets a hint to use it: read the skill, or activate the source. The decision model never enables anything itself; the agent decides, with the usual permissions. Your message and the names and descriptions of your skills and sources are sent to the decision model.
settings.ai.decisions.featureTaskRepairs: Re-run only the steps a failed check points at.

When a task's verification fails without naming the broken steps, Jev/Laya reads the failure reason and judges which steps it points at. Only those steps and the ones that depend on them are repaired, instead of the whole task. With no clear answer the whole task is repaired, as before.
settings.ai.decisions.featureTaskVerdict: When a task verifier forgets the VERDICT line, read the verdict out of its reply instead of asking again.
When a task verifier's reply has no VERDICT line, Jev/Laya reads it as pass, fail or unclear. Only a confident pass or fail is used; otherwise the verifier is asked again.
settings.ai.decisions.featureTurnOutcome: Flag sessions that need you when a turn ends.

After each turn, Jev/Laya reads the agent's last message and judges whether it finished, needs your input, or got stuck. Open sessions that need you move to Needs Review. In task runs, a step that asks a question or gives up is retried or flagged instead of marked done.

tasks.backgroundWorkHint: A subtask counts as done only once its background work ends — a background agent, shell or workflow, a monitor, a scheduled wake-up, an active goal. A scheduled wake-up exists only as the next iteration of a self-paced /loop: a subtask that only asks to be woken has the call refused and schedules nothing. On Codex, a background command started in the subtask's last turn may not be seen before the subtask is marked done, and an agent left running after its turn is waited for, but its report is not the subtask's output: Codex keeps it for the subtask's next turn. On Claude Code, the subtask waits for the reply written after a background task ends, and that reply is its output.
